blocks.markdown: **The central idea.** RA 8792, the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000, generally removes the legal disadvantage caused solely by electronic form. Its central function is to recognize **electronic data messages, electronic documents and electronic signatures** when they meet statutory requirements. It does not mean that every email is automatically authentic, every click forms a contract, or all electronic evidence is conclusive.

The law asks whether an electronic record can do the job the law ordinarily expects of paper: **show information, be retrieved later, identify or approve the sender where required, be reliable, and be properly attributed**. It still requires **proof, authority, consent and compliance with other applicable law**.

Sections 1–5 state the **title, policy, objectives, application and definitions**. **Sec. 4** applies to **data messages and electronic documents used in commercial and noncommercial activities**, including domestic and international dealings, **subject to statutory exclusions and other laws**. Learn the statutory terms separately — **data message, electronic document, electronic signature, originator, addressee, information system, intermediary and service provider are not interchangeable**.
Legal recognition of electronic documents: Secs. 6–9

**Sec. 6 — functional equivalence.** Information is **not to be denied legal effect, validity or enforceability solely because it is in electronic data message or electronic document form**. Where a law requires information to be in writing, an electronic document can satisfy the requirement if the **statutory accessibility and reliability criteria** are met. The key question is whether it **remains accessible for subsequent reference**, with appropriate integrity safeguards.

**Sec. 7 — electronic signatures.** Legal recognition of electronic signatures turns on the **statutory requirements**. An electronic signature can **identify the person and indicate that person’s approval** when the applicable conditions are met. Do not assume every typed name, scanned image or account login is automatically a legally sufficient signature in every situation; assess **reliability, intent, attribution and the relevant transaction**.

**Sec. 8 — retention.** A requirement to retain documents can be met electronically when the information **remains accessible for later reference** and the statutory conditions are satisfied, including **retaining the document in the required form** and related **origin, destination and time information** where applicable.
**Sec. 9 — evidentiary weight.** Evidentiary weight and presumptions depend on the **statute and reliability context**; **authenticity can still be challenged**.

**Functional-equivalence checklist:**

- Ask whether the law requires **“writing,” “signature,” “original,” or “retention”**; each requirement has a distinct functional-equivalence rule.
- Ask if the record can be **retrieved and reproduced accurately later**.
- Ask **who generated, sent or received it, what controls were used, and whether its integrity is reliable**.
- Check if **another statute or type of instrument has a special formality** that the E-Commerce Act does not displace.

An electronic record is **not self-proving** simply because it exists. Under the **Rules on Electronic Evidence** and applicable substantive rules, the proponent may need to establish **authenticity, integrity, source, custody, and reliability**. The statutory recognition in RA 8792 is **not a blanket presumption that the content is true**.

blocks.markdown: The syllabus references **confidentiality and lawful access (Secs. 31–32)**. In application, separate **(1) whether the record is legally recognized, (2) whether its contents are admissible and authentic, and (3) whether accessing, disclosing or using it is lawful**. A party may have a valid electronic document but **obtain it through an unlawful act**, or may **lawfully access a message yet fail to prove its authenticity**.
**Do not confuse an electronic document with an electronic signature.** The record and the identify-and-approve function answer different functional-equivalence questions.
**Do not confuse legal effect with authenticity or truth.** Recognition answers whether electronic form defeats the record; authentication and weight are separate evidentiary questions.

**Check before exam.** Section references reflect the syllabus’ outline. For a fact pattern, **open the full statutory text and the Rules on Electronic Evidence**; the legal answer can turn on exact **system, attribution, integrity and timing facts**.
